courses.title: CARSI Contaminated-Water Practitioner
courses.description:
An Australian-produced credential course for restoration technicians and supervisors in Australia and New Zealand who respond to grossly contaminated water: sewage overflows, failed septic systems and flood water. It treats Category 3 as the health-and-safety job it is, and builds sound field judgement; it is no substitute for a technician’s own certification, a manufacturer’s instructions, a Safety Data Sheet or a site’s own rules.

Six modules follow one job from the call to the handover: what Category 3 water is and how it makes people sick; the law and the risk assessment on both sides of the Tasman (model WHS laws, Victoria’s OHS Act and New Zealand’s Health and Safety at Work Act 2015); PPE, hygiene and decontamination; containment, removal, and cleaning then disinfecting with products legal to use in Australia or New Zealand; lawful disposal of wastewater and waste; and drying, clearance and a defensible job file. Every lesson has a field scenario, a diagram, a worked example in metric units, a one-page field tool and a module check. A practical task and a final designation exam close the course.

CARSI Contaminated-Water Practitioner is a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation. Standards are referenced by name only (for example, aligned to the principles in ANSI/IICRC S500:2025); no standard text is reproduced.
courses.shortDescription: An Australian-produced credential course for Australia and New Zealand, leading to the CARSI Contaminated-Water Practitioner designation: Category 3 sewage and black-water work from the risk assessment and biohazard PPE to containment, cleaning, lawful disposal, drying and a defensible job file.

modules.title: Module 1: Category 3 Water and Why It Is Different

lessons.title: Category 3 water: what it is and how you make the call
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A Tuesday call-out in Ipswich, Queensland. A blocked sewer main has surcharged through the floor waste of a 1970s brick-veneer home. Brown water with toilet paper and solids sits across the bathroom, hallway and the main bedroom carpet. The owner has already mopped with a bath towel and wants the carpet “just dried”. In Lower Hutt, New Zealand, a crew faces the same picture after a stream breaks its banks. Both jobs start with the same question: what water is this, and what does that decide?

The idea

Restorers sort water by how contaminated it is likely to be, because contamination, not the amount of water, decides the method. CARSI teaches the three-category model the industry uses, aligned to the principles in ANSI/IICRC S500:2025, cited by name only. Category 1 is clean water from a sanitary source, Category 2 is significantly contaminated (“grey”) water, and Category 3 is grossly contaminated (“black”) water that can carry harmful bacteria, viruses, parasites and chemicals. The exact wording of those definitions sits in the licensed standard, which your SME holds; this course teaches the field habit, not the text.

On Australian and New Zealand jobs, Category 3 usually arrives through four doors. Sewage: a toilet overflow carrying waste from beyond the trap, a blocked or surcharging sewer, or a broken drain. Failed on-site systems: a septic tank or drainage field backing up, common on regional and rural blocks. Flood and rising water: river, creek and stormwater flooding or a sea surge. Health authorities on both sides of the Tasman tell the public to assume floodwater is contaminated with sewage: NSW Health warns floodwater and debris may carry sewage, and Health New Zealand says to assume floodwater holds farm run-off, animal and human sewage and chemicals. Water that has worsened: Category 1 or 2 water left standing, or water that has run through contaminated material, can become Category 3.

Three habits make the call defensible. First, look for the source, not just the water: where did it come from, what did it pass through, and how long has it sat? Second, when the evidence is mixed, call the worse category and write down why. A crew that treats grey water as black loses some efficiency; a crew that treats black water as grey can make people sick. Third, record the call at the time: photos of the source, the water line and any solids, the time of loss as the owner reports it, and your reasons.

The category decides everything that follows. Category 3 is a health-and-safety job that happens to involve water. It means a documented risk assessment before entry, PPE for a biohazard, containment, removal of porous material that cannot be cleaned, cleaning then disinfecting what stays, lawful disposal, and only then drying. Drying a contaminated structure first locks the problem in and can spread it.

The towel the Ipswich owner used is now contaminated waste, and so are their hands. Your first conversation is about keeping people, especially children and anyone unwell, out of the affected rooms.

See it

Four different doors lead into the same job. Whatever the source, the response is decontamination first.

Do it in metric

Size the Ipswich loss before you quote or plan PPE. Bathroom 2.4 m × 1.8 m = 4.32 m². Hallway 6.0 m × 1.1 m = 6.60 m². Bedroom 3.6 m × 3.0 m = 10.80 m². Affected floor area = 4.32 + 6.60 + 10.80 = 21.72 m². The water line on the skirting averages 15 mm (0.015 m), so the standing volume is about 21.72 × 0.015 = 0.33 m³, or about 330 L of Category 3 water before the carpet’s share. Those figures are illustrative; on a real job you measure them, and they feed the extraction plan, the wastewater route (Module 5) and the job file.

Field download

The Category 3 first-attendance card walks the source check, the category call and its reasons, the area and volume sums, and who must be kept out.

Check yourself

The Module 1 check asks you to identify Category 3 sources, decide what to do when the evidence is mixed, and size a loss in square metres. Each answer explains why.

Takeaway

Category is decided by the source and its history, not by how the water looks; when unsure, call it worse and record why. Category 3 means decontaminate before you dry. Next lesson: how this water makes people sick.

Sources for this lesson

  • NSW Health, Staying healthy during and after flood. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Health New Zealand, Floods and health. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: How Category 3 water makes people sick
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A Lismore, New South Wales, crew is three days into a flood strip-out. The mains water is off, so hand-washing has slipped to a squirt of sanitiser before smoko. One technician has a graze on his forearm from a skirting nail and rolled his sleeves up in the heat. A week later he is off work with a fever and aching muscles, and his GP asks what he has been working in. Across the Tasman, an Auckland crew lead asks whether her team should be vaccinated before the next sewage job.

The idea

Category 3 water is dangerous because of what lives in it. Sewage and floodwater can carry bacteria, viruses and parasites from human and animal waste, plus chemicals picked up on the way. Queensland Health notes floodwater is often contaminated by sewerage, animal and household waste and can cause skin infections, diarrhoea and conjunctivitis. The hazard does not stop when the water drains: silt and mud hold the same contamination, and Health New Zealand warns that dried silt can become airborne and be breathed in.

There are three routes in. Swallowing: hand to mouth, by eating, drinking, smoking or vaping with dirty hands or gloves. Skin and eyes: through cuts, grazes and splashes. Leptospirosis, spread by the urine of infected animals, enters through cuts, open wounds, or the eyes, nose or mouth (Queensland Government), and tetanus enters through big or small wounds. Breathing: aerosols from spraying or water blasting, dust from dried silt, and later, mould spores. Every control you will learn blocks one or more of these routes: gloves and hygiene stop swallowing, covered cuts and fluid-resistant PPE protect skin and eyes, and low-aerosol methods plus a fitted respirator protect the lungs.

Some people are at higher risk. Health New Zealand lists the very young, the very old and people with underlying medical conditions as at higher risk from floodwater illness. Keep them, and anyone pregnant or with a weakened immune system, out of the work area and away from the job until it is cleared. A worker with an uncovered wound is also at higher risk until the wound is covered with a waterproof dressing.

Vaccination is part of the plan in both countries. The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends that plumbers and other workers in regular contact with untreated sewage receive hepatitis A and tetanus vaccines. In New Zealand, the Immunisation Handbook recommends hepatitis A vaccine, unfunded, for occupational groups exposed to faeces, naming sewage workers, and notes it may be employer-funded. Your employer’s occupational health provider or your GP decides what you need; the course does not give medical advice.

Work-related infection is also a legal event. In both countries, a serious infection that work contributed to, including one from contact with human body substances, can be a notifiable event (Module 2). If you feel unwell after a sewage or flood job, tell your supervisor and your doctor what you were working in. For poisoning or chemical exposure advice, call 13 11 26 in Australia or 0800 764 766 in New Zealand; in New Zealand, Healthline (0800 611 116) also gives health advice. In an emergency, call 000 or 111.

See it

Every control in this course blocks one of these three routes.

Do it in metric

With the mains off, plan clean water for hygiene. The Lismore crew is four technicians. Allow (as an illustrative planning figure) six full hand-and-face washes each per day at 2 L per wash: 4 × 6 × 2 L = 48 L per day. That is two 25 L jerry cans (50 L) of clean water with soap at the decontamination point, refilled daily, plus a separate container for waste wash water, which is itself contaminated and goes with the extracted water (Module 5).

Field download

The Category 3 first-attendance card includes a people-at-risk check and the AU and NZ numbers for poisons, health advice and emergencies.

Check yourself

The Module 1 check asks you to name the three exposure routes, who must be kept out, and what vaccines the AU and NZ handbooks recommend for sewage workers.

Takeaway

Category 3 harms people by mouth, through skin and eyes, and by breath; each control blocks a route. Cover cuts, wash before eating, and keep vulnerable people out. Next module: the law and the risk assessment.

modules.title: Module 2: The Law and the Risk Assessment (Australia and New Zealand)

lessons.title: The law on both sides of the Tasman
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A restoration company based on the Gold Coast wins a panel contract that sends crews to Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne and, after a cyclone, to Gisborne in New Zealand. The operations manager wants one Category 3 procedure for every crew. The safety adviser warns that the law, the regulator and the paperwork are not identical in each place, and that a technician who catches an infection on the job triggers duties that differ in wording, not in seriousness.

The idea

Both countries build workplace safety on the same idea. In Australia, the model Work Health and Safety (WHS) laws, maintained by Safe Work Australia, have been implemented in every jurisdiction except Victoria. Under them the person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) has the primary duty of care for workers’ health and safety, and must eliminate risks so far as is reasonably practicable, or if that is not possible, minimise them. Victoria’s main law is the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004, regulated by WorkSafe Victoria, where the duty holder is usually the employer. In New Zealand, the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 (HSWA) puts the same primary duty on the PCBU, and its General Risk and Workplace Management Regulations 2016 set out the hierarchy of controls. A duty cannot be handed to someone else: a subcontract does not move it.

The hierarchy is the same on both sides. Eliminate the hazard if you can. If not, substitute, isolate or engineer it out. Then use administrative controls, and last, PPE. New Zealand’s regulation 6 says that if a risk still remains after the other controls, the PCBU minimises it with suitable PPE. Under regulation 15, the PCBU that directs the work must provide the PPE. On a sewage job, “eliminate” often means removing contaminated porous material, and “isolate” means containment.

The paperwork differs. In Australia, a safe work method statement (SWMS) is required before high-risk construction work starts. Several high-risk categories turn up on Category 3 jobs: work that is likely to disturb asbestos, work in or near a confined space, work near energised electrical installations, and work in an area that may have a contaminated or flammable atmosphere. Whether a given strip-out counts as construction work is a question for your regulator; many restorers write a SWMS for every Category 3 job anyway. In New Zealand, record the same risk assessment in the format your PCBU uses, and check WorkSafe New Zealand guidance for your task.

Infection is notifiable in both countries. Australia’s model WHS Regulations (regulation 699) list, as a serious illness, an infection to which work significantly contributed, including one reliably attributable to contact with human blood or body substances, and leptospirosis from contact with animal waste. The PCBU reports a notifiable incident to the regulator immediately after becoming aware of it and preserves the site. In New Zealand, HSWA section 23 includes a serious infection to which work is a significant contributing factor, including work with micro-organisms or contact with human blood or bodily substances. The PCBU notifies WorkSafe as soon as possible (0800 030 040), preserves the site, and keeps a record for at least five years. In Victoria, check WorkSafe Victoria’s own notification rules.

See it

The words differ by country; the habit is the same: eliminate, else minimise, and record it.

Do it in metric

The procedure must still work at the scale of a real job. The Gisborne house was built in 1994 and extended in 2003; the Brisbane house was built in 1986. Both fall inside the asbestos assumption for their country. In New Zealand it is any building built or renovated before 2000, which covers the original 1994 build. In Australia, assume asbestos may be present in any building built or renovated before 31 December 2003, when the national ban took effect; buildings built or renovated before 1990, like the 1986 Brisbane house, are the most likely to contain it. So both risk assessments assume asbestos in the linings until checked. The planned cut in Gisborne is a 1.2 m-high strip along 9.0 m of internal wall: 1.2 × 9.0 = 10.8 m² of lining that must not be broken until a competent person has checked it. The 2003 extension sits after New Zealand’s before-2000 date, but you still check the original walls it joins.

Field download

The Category 3 risk assessment and SWMS prompts card lists the high-risk triggers to check, the AU and NZ notification steps, and the stop-work points.

Check yourself

The Module 2 check asks who holds the primary duty in each country, when a SWMS is required in Australia, and what makes an infection notifiable.

Takeaway

Australia and New Zealand share the PCBU duty and the hierarchy of controls; the paperwork and notification wording differ. A work-related infection can be notifiable in both. Next lesson: the hazard walk before entry.

lessons.title: The hazard walk before anyone goes in
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A Christchurch rental has had a sewage backup from the gully trap during a storm. The tenant has left. Water has run under the vinyl in the kitchen and laundry, the subfloor smells strongly of sewage, and the kitchen ceiling under the upstairs bathroom is sagging and stained. A new technician is about to go under the house with a torch to “see how bad it is”. His supervisor stops him at the access hatch.

The idea

On a Category 3 job the first decisions are made from the threshold, before anyone steps in. The hazard walk is a fixed habit of six checks, written into the risk assessment as you go.

1. Stop and look. Note the source, the depth, the smell and who is still inside. Do not wade in to find the source.

2. Make the power safe. Water and 230 V mains are a lethal mix in both countries: Australian supply is 230 V, and New Zealand’s regulations set a nominal 230 V at 50 Hz. Isolate affected circuits at the switchboard and confirm they are dead. Run your own gear through a residual current device (RCD, safety switch). In Australia, portable equipment at a workplace must be RCD-protected, with a trip current of no more than 30 mA on socket outlets up to 20 A, and leads are inspected and tested under AS/NZS 3760. In New Zealand, WorkSafe advises that all electrical equipment on construction sites be RCD-protected, and the Electricity (Safety) Regulations 2010 require protection, such as an RCD, for hand-held appliances used in damp situations. Anything electrical that has been under water stays off until a licensed electrician checks it.

3. Structure and slips. A wet ceiling holding water can come down. Silt, wet vinyl and trailing leads are slip and trip hazards.

4. Asbestos. You cannot tell asbestos by looking. In Australia, assume asbestos may be present in any building built or renovated before 31 December 2003, when the national ban took effect. Buildings built or renovated before 1990 are the most likely to contain it. In New Zealand, assume it in any building built or renovated before 2000. Treat it as present until checked. A licence is needed in Australia to assess or remove asbestos. The optional CARSI asbestos awareness course is the foundation for this check.

5. Confined spaces and sewer gas. Pits, sewers and tanks can build up hydrogen sulphide, and methane in a sewer can push oxygen below safe levels. Safe Work Australia’s confined-spaces code puts safe oxygen at 19.5–23.5 % by volume. A tight subfloor or a septic tank may be a confined space; entry needs a trained crew and a permit system, not a torch and a brave technician.

6. People. Move vulnerable occupants out, and keep children and pets away.

If a hazard cannot be controlled, stop and escalate: a licensed electrician, a structural engineer, a licensed asbestos assessor or a confined-space-trained crew. In an emergency call 000 in Australia or 111 in New Zealand.

See it

Six checks from the doorway. Any one you cannot control is a stop.

Do it in metric

How much is that sagging Christchurch ceiling holding? The stain covers 3.0 m × 2.4 m = 7.2 m². If the ceiling holds an average of 10 mm (0.010 m) of water, that is 7.2 × 0.010 = 0.072 m³ = 72 L. Water weighs about 1 kg per litre, so roughly 72 kg of contaminated water is hanging over the kitchen, before the weight of wet plasterboard. Nobody works under it until it is propped or safely drained from a position out of the drop zone.

Field download

The Category 3 risk assessment and SWMS prompts card follows the same six checks, with a stop-and-escalate column.

Check yourself

The Module 2 check asks you to order the hazard walk, decide when a subfloor is a confined space, and work out the load on a wet ceiling.

Takeaway

Six checks from the threshold: look, power, structure, asbestos, confined spaces, people. Any you cannot control is a stop. Next module: PPE and decontamination.

lessons.title: Module 2 check
Choosing PPE for a biohazard
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A Townsville supervisor is setting up a sewage strip-out in a ground-floor unit on a 31 °C day. One technician has a full beard and his own disposable dust mask. Another wants to work in shorts because “the coveralls are too hot”. A third has a cut on his knuckle from a tile. The supervisor has the risk assessment in one hand and the PPE kit in the other, and needs everyone protected before the first cut is made.

The idea

PPE is the last line of defence, used for the risk left after elimination, isolation and engineering controls. On a Category 3 job it matters because the work itself is hands-on contact with contaminated material. The set is chosen from the hazards in the risk assessment, by exposure route.

Breathing. Strip-out, extraction and cleaning create aerosols and dust. CARSI teaches a P2 or higher respirator for hands-on Category 3 work, stepped up where the assessment calls for it; the minimum is a practice for the SME to confirm. Respirators used at work should comply with AS/NZS 1716, which applies in both countries. A tight-fitting respirator only works if it seals. In Australia, workers must pass a fit test before first wearing a tight-fitting respirator, and again after a change to the face that could affect the seal (SafeWork SA). In New Zealand, WorkSafe recommends fit testing when the respirator is first provided and then at least yearly, or after a significant facial change. In both, the wearer fit-checks each time it goes on. Stubble, even one day’s growth in WorkSafe New Zealand’s words, makes a good seal almost impossible; a bearded worker needs a respirator that does not rely on a face seal, such as a hood-type powered respirator. A disposable dust mask is not a fitted respirator.

Eyes and face. Goggles or a face shield wherever splashing is possible, which on a strip-out is most of the time.

Body. A fluid-resistant coverall, disposable where practical, keeps contamination off skin and clothes. Shorts are not an option on a sewage job.

Hands. Gloves are the most-contaminated item you wear. CARSI teaches an inner glove under a chemical- and fluid-resistant outer glove, so the outer pair can be changed without bare skin touching anything.

Feet. Waterproof boots that can be cleaned, or disposable overboots.

Cuts. Cover every cut with a waterproof dressing before you start; health authorities in both countries give the same advice for flood clean-up.

Heat is the trade-off. A coverall and respirator on a hot day add heat stress, so plan breaks, water and a cool clean area rather than letting people strip off PPE. The PCBU provides the PPE (in New Zealand, regulation 15 says so in terms), and records what was worn.

See it

The set is chosen from the hazards in the risk assessment, and recorded.

Do it in metric

Plan the Townsville kit for a three-day strip-out with three technicians. With an illustrative coverall change at each of four breaks per day: 3 technicians × 4 changes × 3 days = 36 coveralls. Outer gloves change at least as often: another 36 pairs, plus spares for tears, say 50 pairs. At 31 °C, plan the breaks into the schedule: four 15-minute breaks in an 8-hour day is 60 minutes, so budget 7 hours of work per person per day, not 8, when you estimate the 21.7 m² job.

Field download

The PPE and decontamination card lists the set by body area, the fit-test rules for Australia and New Zealand, and the removal order.

Check yourself

The Module 3 check asks about the respirator seal, beards, fit testing in each country and what to do about a cut.

Takeaway

PPE is chosen by exposure route and recorded. A respirator protects only when it is fit-tested and fit-checked; a beard needs a respirator that does not rely on a seal. Next lesson: getting out of the PPE without taking the contamination with you.

lessons.title: Decontamination: getting out clean
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

In a Hamilton, New Zealand, villa, a crew finishes the morning’s strip-out and heads for the van for lunch. One technician pulls off his gloves with his teeth, another walks through the clean lounge in his work boots to reach the front door, and a third leaves the bagged carpet in the hallway “for later”. By the afternoon there are brown boot prints on the lounge carpet, which was dry and clean that morning, and the van’s steering wheel has been touched with dirty hands.

The idea

PPE keeps contamination on the outside. Decontamination is how you take it off without moving it to your skin, the clean part of the house or the van. Done badly, it undoes the job: the contamination you contained in the work area walks out on your boots and gloves.

Set up three zones. The dirty zone is the work area: everything there is treated as contaminated. The transition zone sits at the exit: plastic sheeting on the floor, waste bags, a wash station with clean water and soap, and a bin for used PPE. The clean zone is everything beyond, including the van. Traffic goes one way through the transition zone, and nothing contaminated crosses into the clean zone unbagged.

Take PPE off in an order that keeps the dirtiest items away from your skin. The order CARSI teaches is: knock off gross soil from boots and outer gloves; remove outer gloves into the bag; peel the coverall off, rolling it inside out; step out of boots or overboots at the line; remove goggles, then the respirator, by the straps without touching the front; remove inner gloves last; then wash hands and face with soap and water. Bag and seal the waste in the transition zone and take it out by the controlled route. This order is CARSI practice for the SME to confirm against site procedures.

Hygiene sits on top of the routine. Health advice in both countries is consistent: wash hands thoroughly after handling contaminated items, and before eating, drinking or smoking. Health New Zealand adds vaping to that list. Do not touch your face in the work area. Cover cuts before you start. Never eat in the van in your work clothes.

Tools and equipment need the same discipline. Hard tools are cleaned and disinfected before they leave the transition zone, or are bagged for cleaning at the depot. Hoses and wands used for extraction are contaminated inside and out. Vehicles carry contaminated equipment in a separate, cleanable area, not on the passenger seat.

If something goes wrong, such as a needle-stick, a cut through a glove or a splash to the eyes or mouth, stop, decontaminate, wash the area, and seek medical advice the same day. Record it, and tell your supervisor; a resulting serious infection may be notifiable (Module 2).

See it

One way through, one order of removal, every time.

Do it in metric

Size the Hamilton transition zone. The hallway outside the work area is 1.1 m wide; lay sheeting 1.1 m × 2.0 m = 2.2 m², enough for one person to undress and one bag. With four technicians each leaving the work area four times a day, that is 4 × 4 = 16 exits; at an illustrative 4 minutes per exit, decontamination takes 16 × 4 = 64 minutes of crew time per day. Put it in the estimate rather than letting it be skipped.

Field download

The PPE and decontamination card has the zone layout and the removal order as a tick-list for the transition zone.

Check yourself

The Module 3 check asks you to order PPE removal, decide where waste is bagged, and say what to do after a cut through a glove.

Takeaway

Three zones, one way through, one removal order, and wash before you eat. Decontamination time goes in the estimate. Next module: containment, removal and cleaning.

Sources for this lesson

  • NSW Health, Staying healthy during and after flood. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Health New Zealand (HealthEd), Cleaning up a flooded home HE2949. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Immunisation Handbook, Vaccination for people at occupational risk. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Module 3 check

modules.title: Module 4: Containment, Removal, Cleaning and Products

lessons.title: Containment, extraction and what comes out
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

Back at the Ipswich sewage job. The bathroom, hallway and bedroom are affected; the lounge, kitchen and two other bedrooms are dry and clean. The ducted air-conditioning return grille is in the hallway ceiling. The owner asks why the crew is taping plastic across the hallway instead of “getting the carpet up”, and whether the hallway plasterboard can just be wiped down.

The idea

Containment comes before disturbance. Pulling up sewage-soaked carpet, cutting plasterboard and extracting water all throw contamination into the air and onto surfaces. If the work area is open to the rest of the house, the contamination goes there too. On the Ipswich job, the ducted air-conditioning return in the hallway would draw contaminated air through the whole system, so it is turned off and sealed first.

Containment has three parts. Isolate the space: close doors, seal openings and the doorway with plastic sheeting and a zip door, and seal or switch off HVAC. Control the air: an air filtration device (AFD) with a HEPA filter exhausts air from the work area to outside, away from windows, people and air intakes. Exhausting more air than leaks back in keeps the work area at a slightly lower pressure, so leaks flow inwards; you can see it working when the doorway sheeting bows in towards the work area. Control the route: people, waste and equipment move only through the transition zone (Module 3). Low-aerosol methods matter too. Health New Zealand advises against high-pressure hoses or water blasters on sewage-contaminated areas because they spread contaminants into the air.

Then extract. Remove standing water with a contaminated-water extractor or pump, keeping the waste in closed tanks and logging the volume for the wastewater record (Module 5).

Then decide what comes out. Porous materials soaked with Category 3 water, such as carpet and underlay, plasterboard, insulation, particleboard and upholstered furniture, are generally removed and discarded because contamination penetrates them and cleaning cannot be verified. Non-porous materials, such as glazed tile, metal, glass and sealed concrete, are usually cleaned, disinfected and kept. Semi-porous materials such as solid timber are judged case by case. The detail of that decision for Category 3 sits in ANSI/IICRC S500:2025 and is for your SME to confirm; public health advice points the same way. NSW Health advises removing wet floor coverings, furniture and bedding where possible, and Health New Zealand says wooden and plastic kitchen items that touched floodwater cannot be safely cleaned and should be thrown out.

Cut plasterboard above the highest point the water or wicking reached, confirmed with a moisture meter, so no contaminated material is left in the wall. Bag or wrap waste at the point of removal and take it out through the transition zone. Removal is what actually lowers the hazard; cleaning follows it, not instead of it.

See it

Air moves one way: from the clean side, through the work area, through the filter, outside.

Do it in metric

Size the Ipswich AFD. The work area is 21.72 m² with a 2.4 m ceiling: 21.72 × 2.4 = 52.1 m³. For an illustrative target of 4 air changes per hour, the AFD must move 52.1 × 4 = 208 m³/h through its HEPA filter, with the exhaust ducted out. A unit rated at 500 m³/h on low speed meets that with headroom for a loaded filter. Now the plasterboard: wicking reached 450 mm, so the cut line is set at 600 mm along 14.0 m of affected wall: 0.6 × 14.0 = 8.4 m² of plasterboard to remove.

Field download

The removal and cleaning record logs containment set-up, the AFD and its air-change sum, each material removed with its area, and why.

Check yourself

The Module 4 check asks why containment comes first, how to tell negative pressure is working, and which materials usually come out.

Takeaway

Contain before you disturb, keep the air moving one way, and remove what cannot be cleaned. Removal lowers the hazard; cleaning follows it. Next lesson: cleaning and disinfecting what stays.

Sources for this lesson

  • Health New Zealand (HealthEd), Cleaning up a flooded home HE2949. Read 02/11/2026.
  • NSW Health, Staying healthy during and after flood. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Clean, then disinfect, with products legal to use here
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

The Ipswich bathroom tiles, the bedroom’s concrete slab and the hallway’s timber door frames are staying. A technician grabs a spray bottle of disinfectant, mists the slab while it is still coated in brown film, and moves on. A second technician, unsure of the dilution, adds a cap of bleach to a bucket that already had a different cleaner in it. The supervisor stops both of them.

The idea

Once the porous material is out, every surface that stays is cleaned and then disinfected, in that order. Cleaning is mechanical: detergent and water, scrubbing or wiping, removes the soil, the film and most of the micro-organisms with it. Disinfectant is chemical, and it cannot reach organisms protected under dirt. Health advice on both sides of the Tasman gives the same order. NSW Health says hard surfaces should be cleaned with hot soapy water and then disinfected. Health New Zealand says first wash surfaces with detergent and water, then disinfect.

Disinfect to the label, not by guesswork. The label sets the dilution, the contact time (how long the surface must stay wet), whether to rinse, and the PPE. Health New Zealand’s public flood advice, for example, gives two cups (500 mL) of household bleach in 10 L of water, left on for 10–30 minutes or as the product instructions say. Professional products have their own labels; follow yours. Never mix products. Mixing bleach with acids or ammonia-based cleaners can release dangerous gases, which is why every health authority repeats the rule.

Use products that are legal to use and to claim here. In Australia, disinfectants for hard and soft surfaces are regulated by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA). A disinfectant that makes a specific claim, such as killing viruses, must be included in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods before it is supplied; one that makes no specific claim is exempt from listing but must still meet the TGA standard (TGO 104). Some sanitisers fall under the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) instead. In New Zealand, a hazardous substance supplied to a workplace comes with a HSNO-compliant safety data sheet (SDS), and WorkSafe New Zealand says you must hold a current SDS for every hazardous substance in the workplace. In Australia, keep copies of the SDS for the hazardous chemicals you use in your hazardous chemicals register. Do not rely on an overseas registration as if it applied here.

Record what you used: the product name, its registration or approval where it has one, the dilution, the contact time, and the area treated. That record is part of the defensible file (Module 6), and the client or insurer may ask for it.

Timber framing, concrete and other semi-porous materials that stay get the same clean-then-disinfect treatment, then drying. If they cannot be cleaned to a visibly clean, sound surface, they are reassessed for removal.

See it

Disinfectant does not work through dirt. Clean first, then disinfect to the label.

Do it in metric

Mix for the 10.8 m² Ipswich bedroom slab, the 4.32 m² bathroom floor and 6.6 m² of hallway slab: 10.8 + 4.32 + 6.6 = 21.72 m². Suppose the label (illustrative) says 1 part concentrate to 20 parts water and an application rate of 1 L of mixed solution per 5 m². Mixed solution needed: 21.72 ÷ 5 = 4.3 L; round up to a 5 L batch. Concentrate: 5 L ÷ 21 parts = about 240 mL, topped up with clean water to 5 L. Contact time on the label: 10 minutes, so the floor stays wet for 10 minutes before the next step.

Field download

The removal and cleaning record has a product line for each product: name, registration or approval, SDS held, dilution, contact time and area.

Check yourself

The Module 4 check asks why cleaning comes before disinfecting, what a contact time is, and what the TGA requires of a disinfectant that claims to kill viruses.

Takeaway

Clean first, then disinfect to the label, never mix products, and record what you used. Use products legal to use and claim in Australia or New Zealand. Next module: getting rid of the water and waste lawfully.

Sources for this lesson

  • NSW Health, Staying healthy during and after flood. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Health New Zealand (HealthEd), Cleaning up a flooded home HE2949. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Health New Zealand, Floods and health. Read 02/11/2026.
  • TGA, Understanding regulation of disinfectants, sterilants and sanitary products. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Safety data sheets. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Using safety data sheets. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Module 4 check

modules.title: Module 5: Wastewater, Waste and Lawful Disposal

lessons.title: Wastewater: sewer, tanker, never stormwater
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

The Ipswich extractor tank is full of brown water. The nearest drain is the stormwater grate on the driveway, two metres from the van. A technician says “it’s all going to the same place anyway” and reaches for the hose. In Auckland, a crew on a flooded commercial basement has 2,000 L of sewage-contaminated water to remove and wonders whether they can pump it into the building’s gully trap.

The idea

It is not all going to the same place. Stormwater and sewage are separate systems in most Australian and New Zealand cities. Sewage goes through the sewer to a treatment plant. Stormwater, the gutters, grates and pipes that carry rain, goes untreated to creeks, rivers, bays and the sea. EPA Victoria says stormwater is not treated before it reaches waterways, and Watercare says Auckland’s collected stormwater empties directly into streams and the sea. Pouring Category 3 water down a stormwater grate puts raw sewage into a waterway. In Auckland, the Stormwater Bylaw prohibits discharging any substance into the public stormwater system.

That leaves two lawful routes.

To the sewer, with approval. Water from a business activity going into the sewer is trade waste (trade wastewater), and the water authority or council controls it. EPA Victoria says businesses need a trade waste agreement with the local water authority to discharge trade waste to a sewer. Sydney Water says businesses must seek formal approval to discharge commercial trade wastewater. In New Zealand, councils control trade waste through bylaws: Auckland’s Trade Waste Bylaw requires higher-risk trade waste to have council approval through a trade waste agreement, and Watercare says a one-off discharge may need its own agreement or provisional consent. Rules differ between authorities, so ask before you pump: call the water authority or council, explain the source and volume, and get the answer in writing.

To a liquid-waste contractor. Where no approval is in place, or the volume is large, a contractor pumps the water into a tanker and takes it to a facility that accepts it. Use a contractor who holds whatever licence or permit your state EPA or regional council requires, and keep the docket.

The building’s own plumbing is not a shortcut. Pumping into a gully trap or toilet is still a discharge to the sewer, it can overload a drain that may already be the cause of the problem, and repairs to sanitary plumbing and drains are licensed work in both countries. In New Zealand, the Plumbers, Gasfitters, and Drainlayers Act 2006 says a person must not do sanitary plumbing or drainlaying unless authorised. A blocked or broken drain goes to a licensed plumber or drainlayer, and a blocked public sewer to the water authority or council.

Write down every litre. The wastewater record is part of the defensible file: volume, route, approval or docket number, date and who took it.

See it

Two lawful routes and one banned one. Ask the water authority or council before you pump.

Do it in metric

Plan the Ipswich wastewater. The estimate from Module 1 was about 330 L of standing water; add an illustrative 20 % for water held in the carpet and wash water: 330 × 1.2 = about 400 L. The extractor recovery tank holds 45 L, so that is 400 ÷ 45 = 8.9, or 9 tank-loads. Each is decanted into sealed 200 L drums for collection (2 drums), not tipped onto the driveway. For the Auckland basement, 2,000 L is 2.0 m³: a job for a tanker under a docket, or for an approval in writing from Watercare before anything goes into the gully trap.

Field download

The waste and wastewater record logs each discharge or collection: litres, route, approval or docket number, date and contractor.

Check yourself

The Module 5 check asks where stormwater goes, who approves a discharge to sewer in each country, and how many tank-loads a volume takes.

Takeaway

Category 3 water goes to the sewer only with approval, or to a liquid-waste contractor, and never to stormwater. Ask first, log every litre. Next lesson: the solid waste.

Sources for this lesson

  • EPA Victoria, Publication 980.1 (stormwater fact sheet). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Watercare (Auckland), Wastewater FAQs. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Auckland Council, Trade Waste Bylaw 2013. Read 02/11/2026.
  • EPA Victoria, Preventing stormwater pollution: a guide for industry. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Sydney Water, Commercial trade wastewater. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Business Licence and Information Service, Approval to dispose of waste and trade wastewater (NSW). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Watercare (Auckland), Trade waste agreements. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Plumbers, Gasfitters, and Drainlayers Act 2006 (NZ). Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Solid waste, asbestos and the paper trail
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A Brisbane crew has stripped a flood-affected 1960s Queenslander: carpet, underlay, the bottom of the plasterboard walls, a laundry cabinet and a pile of used coveralls. Under the laundry vinyl, the technician finds a grey, fibrous backing sheet. The skip bin out the front is half full of everything mixed together, and the neighbour is asking whether she can put her own wet carpet in it too.

The idea

Solid waste from a Category 3 job falls into separate streams, and they are sorted at the point of removal, not at the tip.

Contaminated porous material and used PPE. Carpet, underlay, plasterboard, insulation and disposable PPE are bagged or wrapped where they come out, sealed, and taken through the transition zone to a covered skip or vehicle. Double-bagging contains leaks. The receiving facility must accept the waste type; call ahead, because landfills and transfer stations set their own requirements, especially after a flood. The NSW Government tells flood-affected residents to check their local landfill for special requirements for flood-damaged waste, and the same check applies to a business load.

Suspected asbestos. The grey backing under the Brisbane vinyl may be asbestos: the house was built well before 1990. Stop work on that material. Do not break, cut or sweep it, and do not put it in the general skip. A licensed asbestos assessor confirms it, and in Australia a licence is needed to remove it; the asbestos waste goes to a facility licensed to take it. In New Zealand, apply the before-2000 rule of thumb and follow WorkSafe New Zealand’s asbestos requirements. Mixing asbestos into the general skip contaminates the whole load.

Chemical containers. Empty and part-used product containers are disposed of as the label and SDS say. Nothing goes down the stormwater.

The skip is yours while it is on your job. A neighbour’s waste in your skip becomes your load at the weighbridge, and it may not be what your docket says. Keep the skip covered and in your control.

Every stream gets a docket: facility name, date, weight or volume, and the vehicle or contractor. With the wastewater record from the last lesson, the dockets prove that what came out of the building went somewhere lawful. Insurers and loss adjusters ask for them, and a regulator may too.

Where the job is near an on-site wastewater system (a septic tank and drainage field), the system itself may be damaged by the flood. NSW Health advises having septic systems inspected after flooding and seeking council advice; in New Zealand, Health New Zealand lists sewage backing up in toilets and drains as a sign of a flooded septic tank. That inspection is the owner’s plumber’s or council’s job, not the restorer’s, but you note it in the report.

See it

Sort at the point of removal. Three streams, never mixed, each with a docket.

Do it in metric

Estimate the Brisbane waste volume before ordering the skip. Carpet and underlay: 48 m² at about 20 mm combined thickness = 48 × 0.020 = 0.96 m³. Plasterboard: 0.6 m cut × 32 m of wall × 0.010 m = 0.19 m³. Laundry cabinet and PPE bags: allow 1.0 m³. Loose volume is larger than solid volume; with an illustrative bulking factor of 1.5: (0.96 + 0.19 + 1.0) × 1.5 = 2.15 × 1.5 = 3.2 m³. A 4 m³ skip fits, with the asbestos backing kept out of it entirely.

Field download

The waste and wastewater record has a docket line for each solid-waste stream and an asbestos hold box.

Check yourself

The Module 5 check asks how waste streams are kept apart, what to do with suspected asbestos, and how to size a skip.

Takeaway

Sort at the point of removal into three streams, keep asbestos out of the skip, and keep a docket for every load. Next module: drying, verification and the job file.

Sources for this lesson

  • NSW Government, Storm and flood clean-up assistance and advice. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Asbestos overview. Read 02/11/2026.
  • NSW Government (asbestos.nsw.gov.au), When was asbestos banned in Australia?. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Asbestos in Aotearoa New Zealand. Read 02/11/2026.
  • NSW Health, Beware of environmental health risks in flood clean up (25/03/2021). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Health New Zealand, Floods and health. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Module 5 check

modules.title: Module 6: Drying, Clearance, the Job File and the Designation

lessons.title: Drying after decontamination, and the mould rule
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

The Ipswich job is cleaned and disinfected. The slab, the bottom plates of the timber frame and the remaining wall linings are still wet. The project manager wants air movers in today to hit the insurer’s timeline. A technician points out a patch of fuzzy grey growth on the back of a bedroom built-in robe that nobody saw at the first visit, eleven days after the loss.

The idea

On a Category 3 job, drying comes after decontamination. You dry a clean structure, not a contaminated one. Air movers blowing across dirty material spread it; heat and airflow on a contaminated surface can also make the contamination harder to remove. So the order is: contain, remove, clean and disinfect, verify clean, and then dry. That order sits in the principles of ANSI/IICRC S500:2025; how it is worded there is for your SME to confirm from the licensed copy.

Once surfaces are verified clean, drying follows the same principles as any water job: set a dry standard from unaffected material of the same type, use dehumidification to take water out of the air, use controlled airflow across wet surfaces, and monitor with a moisture meter and thermo-hygrometer until materials reach the dry standard. The CARSI Water Restoration Practitioner and Structural Drying courses teach that method in full.

The mould rule. If mould is present, the airflow decision changes. Do not run air movers across mouldy surfaces. Contain the area, run AFDs and dehumidifiers to control moisture without blowing spores around, remediate the mould, and bring in air movers only once the area is cleaned and cleared. Public health advice supports the reason: Queensland Health warns that dry brushing mould can release spores into the air. SafeWork NSW advises discarding porous materials that cannot be readily cleaned or have been wet for more than 48 hours. The robe panel in Ipswich is porous, wet and mouldy, so it comes out, bagged, inside containment. The mould rule in this form is CARSI practice for the SME to confirm.

Power is the practical limit on drying. Australian and New Zealand supply is 230 V, and a typical 10 A general power outlet (GPO) circuit carries at most 10 A. Too much load trips the circuit breaker, which cuts the power to protect the wiring. Several outlets often share one circuit, so a power budget per circuit is part of the drying plan, with every lead tested and tagged and run through an RCD.

Verify dry with readings, not by feel: the same points, the same meter, recorded against the dry standard, until stable. Only then do new linings and floor coverings go back.

See it

Drying is the last stage of a Category 3 job, not the first.

Do it in metric

Budget the Ipswich drying power. Planned equipment (illustrative rating-plate currents at 230 V): two dehumidifiers at 4.5 A each and one AFD at 2.5 A. Total: 4.5 + 4.5 + 2.5 = 11.5 A, more than one 10 A circuit can carry. Split it: dehumidifier 1 plus the AFD on circuit A = 7.0 A; dehumidifier 2 on circuit B = 4.5 A. Power drawn: 230 V × 11.5 A = 2,645 W, about 2.6 kW. Air movers come later, after clearance, and need their own budget.

Field download

The clearance and job-file checklist has the drying power budget table and the mould hold box.

Check yourself

The Module 6 check asks when drying starts on a Category 3 job, what changes when mould is found, and how to split a power load across 10 A circuits.

Takeaway

Decontaminate first, then dry. If mould is found, AFDs and dehumidifiers only until it is cleaned and cleared. Budget power per 10 A circuit. Next lesson: clearance and the defensible file.

Sources for this lesson

  • Queensland Health, Mould (public health advice). Read 02/11/2026.
  • SafeWork NSW, Mould. Read 02/11/2026.
  • NSW Government, Voltage optimisation fact sheet. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Electricity (Safety) Regulations 2010 (NZ). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Electrical Safety Office Queensland, Safety switches. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe ACT, Residual current devices. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Clearance and the defensible job file
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

Six weeks after the Ipswich job, the owner’s daughter, who is pregnant, wants to move back in. She asks the insurer how she can know the house is safe. The loss adjuster asks the restorer for the job file. One company sends a two-line invoice and twenty unlabelled photos. Another sends a dated file showing what was found, what came out, what was used, where the waste went and the readings at handover. Only one of those answers her question.

The idea

A Category 3 job is finished when the area is verified clean, dry and safe to hand over, not when it looks tidy. Clearance is a decision, made on evidence, and recorded.

Verify clean. All contaminated porous material removed; every remaining surface visibly clean, with no soil, film or residue; cleaning and disinfection recorded with product, dilution and contact time; containment still intact until the check is done; photographs of each area. Where the client, insurer or the job’s complexity calls for it, an independent check, such as an occupational hygienist, adds weight. What counts as clearance for Category 3 is for your SME to confirm against ANSI/IICRC S500:2025 and the job’s scope.

Verify dry. Readings at the same points with the same meter, at or below the dry standard and stable, recorded with the date and time.

Hand over. Remove containment and equipment, explain to the occupant in plain words what was done and what to watch for, such as new staining, odour or dampness, and get the handover signed.

The file is built as the job runs, not reconstructed at the end. It holds: the first-attendance call (source, category and why, photos); the risk assessment or SWMS and inductions; the PPE worn; the removal log with areas and reasons; the products used; the wastewater record and waste dockets; the drying readings; any incidents; and the clearance and handover. Records made at the time are what a loss adjuster, a regulator or a court is most likely to accept.

The file also protects the customer’s rights. In Australia, the Australian Consumer Law gives consumers automatic guarantees that services are provided with due care and skill and are fit for any stated purpose. In New Zealand, the Consumer Guarantees Act 1993 requires services to be carried out with reasonable care and skill and to be fit for purpose. Describe the work honestly; a file that shows what was done is how you show the guarantees were met.

Quote and invoice in Australian dollars. In Australia, GST is 10 %; show it.

See it

Records made at the time are the evidence. Build the file as the job runs.

Do it in metric

The Ipswich file summary, in metric: 21.72 m² affected; 21.72 m² carpet and underlay and 8.4 m² plasterboard removed; about 400 L of wastewater to a liquid-waste contractor (2 drums, docket recorded); 5 L of disinfectant solution at 1:20 with a 10-minute contact time; final readings at the dry standard on three consecutive days. Invoice (illustrative): $4,800.00 ex GST; GST 10 % = $480.00; total $5,280.00 AUD inc GST.

Field download

The clearance and job-file checklist lists the eight records, the verify-clean and verify-dry checks, and the handover sign-off.

Check yourself

The Module 6 check asks what clearance needs, why records are made at the time, and what the consumer guarantees require in each country.

Takeaway

Clearance is an evidence-based decision: verify clean, verify dry, hand over, record it. Build the file as you go. Next lesson: preparing your practical submission.

Sources for this lesson

  • ACCC, Consumer rights and guarantees. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Consumer Protection (MBIE), Consumer Guarantees Act. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Taxation Office, How GST works. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Preparing your practical submission and the designation exam
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT v1 for SME review. Scenarios and figures are illustrative; every claim is in the evidence ledger.

On the job

A Launceston technician has finished the six modules and opens the practical task. She has attended plenty of sewage jobs but has never written one up from start to finish. Her first draft is three photos and a paragraph saying the job “went well”. Her assessor in Hobart sends it back with one note: show the decisions, the numbers and the records, as if a loss adjuster in Wellington had to follow it without ringing you.

The idea

The CARSI Contaminated-Water Practitioner designation is earned by showing you can run a whole Category 3 job, not just recall facts. It has two parts after the modules: a practical task, marked by an assessor against a rubric, and the final designation exam. The optional CARSI asbestos awareness course is the recommended foundation. The designation is a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation for Australia and New Zealand.

The practical asks you to plan and evidence one Category 3 job from first attendance to handover: a real job you attended, with identifying details removed, or the supplied scenario. It is marked on five criteria, each worth 20 points, with a pass at 80 %:

  • The category call and the loss size: source, category and why, area in m², volume in litres.
  • Risk assessment and the law: the hazard walk, the controls from the top of the hierarchy down, the SWMS or NZ equivalent, the notification steps for the job’s country.
  • PPE and decontamination: the set by exposure route, fit test and fit check, the three zones and the removal order.
  • Containment, removal, cleaning and waste: containment and the AFD sum, what came out and why, clean-then-disinfect with the product record, the wastewater route and dockets.
  • Drying, clearance and the file: decontamination before drying, the mould rule, a 230 V power budget, clearance evidence, the consumer guarantee, and an AUD invoice with GST.

Write it the way the job ran. Use headings that match the criteria. Show every sum with its units. State the reason for each decision in one sentence. Name standards by title only, and never copy text from any standard. Use Australian English and metric units. If your job was in New Zealand, use the New Zealand law, regulator and numbers; if it was in Australia, name the state and its regulator.

Common reasons for resubmission: no reason given for the category; PPE listed without the fit test; waste “taken away” with no route or docket; drying started before cleaning was verified; power maths at the wrong voltage; photos without captions or dates.

The final exam is 20 questions drawn from all six modules, with a pass mark of 80 %. Each answer has a practitioner’s explanation, so read the “why” on anything you miss before you retake it.

See it

The practical shows you can run the whole job; the exam shows you know why.

Do it in metric

Check your marks before you submit. Five criteria × 20 points = 100 points. The pass is 80 %: 0.80 × 100 = 80 points. If you are confident of 17 on four criteria (68 points), you need at least 12 on the fifth to pass, but a weak criterion is usually where the assessor asks for resubmission, so aim for 16 or more on every one.

Field download

The practical submission checklist maps each criterion to the evidence the assessor looks for.

Check yourself
